#5313. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#5311. New York bans AI toys amid concern after stuffed animals going rogue

New York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” the governor said. “When tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to our kids and our babies, you bet I’m going to have something to say about it.”

Though dangerous dolls manipulating innocent children may sound like the plot of Hollywood movie, recent tests of certain chatbot-powered toys have become a real cause for concern. When journalists at NBC News tested the Pixie Paw, an AI-powered plush cat toy marketed to children aged three and older, it reportedly shared stories of massacres, gang rape and firing squads in what was described as graphic detail.

Other tests have shown some of the toys can become very convincing when trying to persuade the young user that they are human. “Parents have enough to worry about,” said Hochul, who was also aware some of the smart toys have encouraged kids to jump out of windows.

State senator Andrew Gounardes applauded the move, saying that modern life seems to be mimicking science fiction of days gone by. He invoked an episode of the “Twilight Zone that featured the Talky Tina doll, an insidious, possessed toy that tried to persuade a young girl to murder her strict stepfather.

New York Attorney General Letitia James explained that the toys being put on the market is reckless when they clearly expose “young people to inappropriate content and put “their mental health at risk.” She added, “We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”

DUBAI, UAE, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XEBO.ai, an AI-native experience management company, has raised US $10.5 million in funding from Emirates Growth Fund (EGF), the UAE's flagship growth equity investor. EGF becomes its first institutional investor.

The company will use the funds to deepen its voice-of-customer product portfolio, extending it into areas such as call and digital experience analytics, and to advance agentic AI across its platform.

XEBO.ai will also expand its go-to-market across the GCC, establish a presence in the United States and hire senior leaders.

XEBO.ai uses AI to turn customer and employee feedback into decision-ready insights. Its platform spans surveys, social listening and journey mapping across customer experience, employee experience and market research.

The company has served more than 350 organisations across more than 10 industries, including banking, aviation, telecommunications, insurance, retail, public sector and healthcare. Its clients span EMEA, Asia Pacific and North America, and it employs more than 100 people.

The investment sits within EGF's Advanced Technology mandate. Beyond capital, EGF will support XEBO.ai's management on governance, senior hiring and access to its government and private-sector network.

#5308. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5307. DeepL introduces Aure v2, its fastest Voice AI translation model

COLOGNE, Germany, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DeepL, a global leader in Language AI, today launched Aure v2, a breakthrough Voice AI translation model that pushes the boundaries of real-time translation, at its inaugural Unmute Summit in Tokyo. Now available to DeepL Voice customers, Aure v2 reduces translation delays by 50% compared to its predecessor while further increasing translation accuracy and expressiveness, making real-time multilingual conversations faster and more natural.

The launch builds on Aure, DeepL's Voice AI model introduced earlier this month, which made translations more natural by continuously adapting to a speaker's voice, tone, and intonation throughout a conversation. Now, Aure v2 takes the next step, introducing a new end-to-end model architecture and reinforcement learning to dramatically reduce translation delays while increasing accuracy and expressiveness. Together, these advancements bring DeepL closer to driving a future where people can communicate naturally across languages, without delays or misunderstandings getting in the way.

"With Aure v2, we've significantly cut translation delays while also pushing the accuracy and quality of DeepL Voice even further," said Jarek Kutylowski, Founder and CEO, DeepL. "This is a major technical breakthrough, but what's even more exciting is what this makes possible for our customers. In a global meeting, people can respond to ideas as they're shared â or customer service agents can resolve issues faster without losing the nuance of a conversation. These are the moments we're solving for, where speed, reliability and understanding make a huge difference."

Faster conversations with market-leading translation quality

Even the most accurate, expressive translation can disrupt a conversation if it arrives too late. Real-time voice translation requires a careful balance between speed and accuracy: models need enough context to preserve meaning, but waiting too long can interrupt the natural flow of conversation.

Aure v2 significantly advances this balance. In internal benchmarks*, the model achieved:

This combination of speed and accuracy is particularly important in business-critical environments like customer support centers and high-stakes negotiations, where delays can disrupt conversations and misunderstandings can have real business consequences.

A new approach to real-time speech translation

Behind Aure v2's industry-leading performance is a new end-to-end model architecture that translates directly from speech to speech, eliminating the need for separate transcription, translation and speech stages.

Real-time voice translation has traditionally relied on three separate steps: converting speech into text, translating that text into another language, and generating speech from the translation. Each step relies on the previous one, adding processing time and delays that can disrupt the flow of conversations. Aure v2 brings these together into a single step, translating directly from speech to speech and significantly reducing delays.

The breakthrough also goes beyond a faster architecture. One of the biggest challenges in real-time speech translation is knowing when to begin the translation output. Start too early, and important context may be lost, which may result in an inaccurate translation; wait too long, and you might get an accurate translation but the conversation slows down. This is particularly difficult for languages like German and Japanese, where essential information can come at the end of a sentence.

Training a model to make these decisions is challenging because high-quality datasets including recordings of real-time speech translation with the right timing and expression are scarce. Rather than relying on large volumes of this data, DeepL therefore had to resort to reinforcement learning to teach the model how to translate fast and accurately. During training, Aure v2 was rewarded for translations that were both accurate and quick to start. Over time, it learned to recognize when it had heard enough context to begin translating.

"The key to real-time translation isn't simply processing speech faster â it's knowing when you have enough information to translate accurately," said Sebastian Enderlein, Chief Technology Officer, DeepL. "With Aure v2, we've combined a fundamentally new AI architecture with reinforcement learning to tackle both challenges at once. Building on years of DeepL's expertise in how meaning and nuance carry across languages, we're making simultaneous translation faster, more accurate, and closer to the pace of natural conversation."

Built for the enterprise, with adoption accelerating worldwide

Aure v2 comes as DeepL Voice continues to see strong adoption worldwide, with usage up more than 8x year over year in Q3 2026 (total voice minutes) and translated meeting minutes up approximately 7x.

Momentum has been particularly strong in Asia, alongside strong growth in the US and Germany. In Q3 2026, DeepL Voice meeting usage grew more than 7x in Japan and 5x in South Korea YOY, measured by minutes spent in meetings, and was up more than 6x in both the US and Germany. As of October 2026, the number of active DeepL Voice subscriptions with meeting usage had grown approximately 12x YOY in Japan and South Korea combined, 8x in the US and 9x in Germany.

Aure v2 supports six languages at launch: English, German, French, Spanish, Japanese and Korean, with more languages coming soon. The model is now available across DeepL Voice for Online Meetings, DeepL Voice for In-Person Conversations and the DeepL API for Voice, and is automatically enabled for supported languages without additional setup.

To learn more about Aure v2 and try it yourself, visit https://dee.pl/fvtq1.

*Results from DeepL internal study, November 2026, on 1-minute real-speech recordings across 10 language pairs, with human-validated transcripts. All models were tested over public API with no app overhead. Results may differ in real conversations. All third-party product and company names are trademarks of their respective owners. Their use is strictly for identification purposes and does not imply any affiliation with or endorsement by them.

#5305. The midterms showed boomers losing their grip on politics. Their grip on the money is another story

A wave of Democrat support in the midterms swept across the U.S. in the beginning of November marking a change of power in politics—not just from the flipping of red to blue, but also from old to young: non-boomer politicians in Congress are at their highest point since the turn of the century. But even as the Baby Boomers are losing their hold on political power, their economic influence remains considerably more difficult to dislodge.

Americans born between 1946 and 1964 still control more than half of the nation’s wealth, despite representing a continuously shrinking share of the population. And their financial advantage has implications for younger generations struggling with housing costs, student debt and the rising cost of living—especially as the transfer of wealth from older generations to their children remains sluggish.

The shift away from Baby Boomer leadership in government has been building for years, but the 2026 midterms accelerated the transition. For the first time in decades, the generation that dominated congressional leadership and policymaking is losing its grip.

The House already moved past the point of Boomer dominance. According to Pew Research Center, Boomers accounted for 39% of House members at the beginning of the 119th Congress, down from a majority just two Congresses earlier. Gen X became the largest generation in the chamber, representing 41% of lawmakers while Millennials accounted for another 15%. The Senate has been slower to change. Boomers still represent 60 of 99 senators at the beginning of the 119th Congress, or roughly 61%.

But that imbalance is beginning to change. According to Quorum’s analysis of newly elected lawmakers, Gen X and Millennials account for 87% of the incoming 120th Congressional class. Of the 120 new members, just 13 are Boomers—while 56 Gen Xers and 48 Millennials will occupy the new seats.

The change is also visible in the pipeline of candidates seeking office. Future Caucus found that Millennials and Gen Z accounted for roughly one-third of congressional candidates in 2026, up from one-quarter in 2024 and one-sixth in 2022. According to the report, Millennials also became the largest generational group running for Senate for the first time in the report’s history.

Still, the political transition is not complete as the Senate continues to be a stubborn stronghold for older Americans. The incoming chamber’s median age will fall to 63 from 64, but will still remain among the oldest Senates in American history, according to Reuters.

According to the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts, Baby Boomers held approximately $97.4 trillion in household net worth in Q2 2026. That represents 52.5% of all U.S. household wealth, despite Boomers accounting for just 27% of the country’s adult population.

In contrast, Millennials and Gen Z together represented 22.4% of real estate but only held 11.2% of household wealth—about $20.8 trillion. Generation X held another 25.7%.

And while the great wealth transfer is coming, younger Americans are waiting. Visa’s Business and Economic Insights report in July estimated approximately $36 trillion of Baby Boomers’ $93 trillion in assets could transfer to younger generations over the next 20 years—after accounting for liabilities, taxes, fees, retirement spending and other exclusions.

“Imagine you are sitting on a winning lottery ticket. You hit the jackpot, but you immediately lose half by— smartly—taking the lump sum,” the report read. “Next, you lose another 30–40 percent through taxes and fees. The advertised jackpot is enormous, but after the lump-sum haircut, taxes and fees, the take-home number is much lower. A similar dynamic applies to the great wealth transfer.”

But that doesn’t mean the younger Americans will now get access to that same financial security. The transfer is likely to be uneven, with most of the wealth being concentrated among families that already have substantial assets.

According to Visa’s research, nearly 75% of inheritance recipients already have higher net worths than the average household. That means much of the inherited wealth from the transfer will be saved or invested, not immediately spent. Visa also estimated that one in four millennial homeowners received financial assistance from their parents for a down payment.

But perspective matters. A 2025 analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that Millennials and Gen Z households actually had more inflation-adjusted wealth at approximately age 34 than Boomers did at that same age.

According to the analysis, Millennials and Gen Zers owned $1.23 for every $1 of wealth owned by Gen Xers at the same age—and $1.35 for every $1 of wealth owned by baby boomers.

The generational war has a six-year deadline, set by Social Security and the national debt.

According to the 2026 Social Security trustees report, the combined retirement and disability trust funds are projected to be depleted by 2032. At that point, incoming revenue would only cover 83% of scheduled benefits unless Congress changes the program.

Boomers have held the presidency since 2001, spanning George W. Bush to Donald Trump, with the exception of Joe Biden—who is part of the Silent Generation. In that time span, the national debt climbed from $5.81 trillion to over $40.17 trillion through September 2026, according to the Treasury’s fiscal data, during which time, they have passed a series of tax cuts leaving their own generation’s retirements endangered.

Democrats have argued for increasing revenue by raising the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes, while Republicans mostly emphasized economic growth. But Sen. Ron Johnson—the Wisconsin Republican who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and is a Boomer himself—has a typically Boomerian fix: make other generations pay for it.

Social Security is funded primarily through payroll taxes paid by today’s workers, meaning younger Americans now are financing the benefits for current retirees. But once the funds are depleted, covering the shortfall would mean borrowing more from other federal priorities. In effect, the government would be putting the cost of maintaining the retirement benefits on the national credit card, leaving younger taxpayers to help service the debt through future taxes or spending cuts.

On Nov. 18, Johnson called Social Security a “legal Ponzi scheme” on Fox Business. The following day, he said Congress should first pass legislation preventing benefit cuts and then address what he described as the country’s massive debt. He also introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act, allowing the Treasury’s general fund to cover Social Security benefits after it becomes insolvent. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates the approach would add $190 trillion to the federal debt over 75 years.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5304. HONOR X9e Pro introduces features, making the phone tough to beat

KUWAIT CITY, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Choosing a smartphone means looking for the right balance of features, performance and everyday practicality. The best phones are the ones that get the important things right, and the HONOR X9e Pro ticks all the boxes.

From exceptional durability and outstanding battery life to a capable camera, practical AI features and a vibrant display, it brings together everything users look for in a modern smartphone. More importantly, it delivers these features in a sleek, everyday design without compromising on comfort or usability. That combination makes the HONOR X9e Pro a standout choice for those looking for a smartphone that goes beyond expectations.

Phones get dropped. Drinks get spilled. Rain happens.

The HONOR X9e Pro is built with those moments in mind, with protection tested for drops of up to three metres under controlled conditions, alongside IP68, IP69 and IP69K water and dust resistance.

It goes further when conditions get tougher, with the ability to withstand hot-water splashes of up to 85Â°C and submersion in water up to 10 metres. Its battery is also designed to maintain endurance in temperatures of up to 50Â°C, adding another layer of reassurance when the heat is on.

The important part is that all this toughness doesn't turn it into a bulky rugged phone. At around 8.08mm thick and 203g, it still feels made for everyday use.

Then there's the 11,000mAh battery, one of the X9e Pro's biggest everyday advantages.

HONOR rates it for up to three days of use under its defined mixed-usage testing, with 80W HONOR SuperCharge when it eventually needs plugging in. It also supports 27W wired reverse charging, so the X9e Pro can step in to power compatible devices when needed.

Longevity matters too. The battery comes with 6 years durability design, giving the X9e Pro an endurance story that goes beyond simply making it through a long day.

The appeal is simple: less time watching your battery percentage and more freedom to use your phone. Long workdays, travel, navigation, photos and videos all become easier when finding a charger isn't constantly on your mind.

The 108MP main camera adds another reason for the X9e Pro to stand out. It's made for the moments people actually want to capture, from portraits and nights out to holidays and spontaneous shots. CIPA 6.0-level stabilisation helps keep shots steady when shooting on the move, while underwater shooting opens up another creative option for those moments that take you beyond dry land.

The technology works in the background, so the focus can stay where it should: getting the shot.

AI is everywhere in smartphones right now, but the features that matter are the ones that genuinely make the experience better. On the HONOR X9e Pro, AI works across both the camera and display, with features such as AI Image to Video, helping with everyday creativity, while AI Defocus Display and AI Personalised Display are designed to make viewing more comfortable.

Rather than putting AI front and centre for the sake of it, these tools complement the wider experience, helping make capturing content and using the phone feel more intuitive and convenient. It's not the sole reason to choose the X9e Pro, but it adds another layer of everyday usefulness to an already well-rounded phone.

The 6.8-inch display offers smooth scrolling and strong outdoor visibility, while practical touches such as wet-hand and glove touch support come in handy when conditions aren't perfect.

They may not be the headline features, but together they help make the X9e Pro feel like a well-rounded everyday phone.

The X9e Pro's biggest strength isn't any one feature. It's how well everything comes together.

It's tough without feeling rugged, packs an unusually large battery without becoming cumbersome, and still delivers the camera, AI and display experience expected from a modern smartphone.

For anyone looking for serious durability, long-lasting battery life and a well-rounded everyday experience, the HONOR X9e Pro makes a convincing case for itself.

And that combination is exactly what puts it among the phones worth considering.

#5303. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

#5302. Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

Identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

Artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

AgentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

Language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

Permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

AgentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more important point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

The companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. Start the inventory and the permission cleanup now. The tools to enforce the rest are arriving quickly, and they will work far better for the teams that did the groundwork.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5301. Former Pentagon officials say Hegseth blocking senators from visiting Gulf bases amid Iran war ‘smells like a lack of transparency’

The Pentagon is banning U.S. lawmakers from visiting Gulf military bases, and former Pentagon officials warn the move is creating tension between the executive and legislative branches and raising questions about why the Department of Defense is limiting access to information about the Iran war.

“It smells like a lack of transparency in order to thwart Congressional oversight, in order to either hide that the Iran war is costing more, or to use the Iran war as an excuse to get more money,” Evelyn Farkas, executive director of the McCain Institute at Arizona State University and former deputy assistant secretary of defense for Russia, Ukraine, and Eurasia, told Fortune.

Last month, Connecticut Democrat Sen. Chris Murphy detailed his experience of the Department of Defense barring him from visiting the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and meeting with military leadership, accusing the Pentagon of obscuring details about the impacts of the Iran war.

“I have been to the Middle East probably a dozen times at least,” Murphy said in a video uploaded to Facebook. “While I have been a member of Congress, I have never, ever been denied access to military facilities. This is part of a coordinated, deliberate campaign by the Department of Defense to try to hide the consequences and the true cost of this war.”

Iowa Republican Sen. Joni Ernst was similarly turned away from a base visit around the same time, The Atlantic reported this week. Ernst did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

U.S. Congress members have a long-standing practice of conducting visits of military sites as part of their constitutional oversight. In March, following the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth published a memo to “further discourage visits to the [U.S. Central Command Area of Responsibility] requiring DoW support by members of Congress and their staffs…and no DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.”

Congress has expressed increased misgivings around Hegseth, introducing articles of impeachment this month, which did not pass, in part on the grounds that the secretary began military conflict in Iran without Congressional authorization. Hegseth has sharply reduced the number of routine press briefings and limited press access to briefings, as well as refused to provide information to the Congressional Budget Office ahead of its update to the cost of the Iran war in September. Meanwhile, the Pentagon is seeking $1.5 trillion in allocations—the largest defense budget in U.S. history—to modernize military infrastructure and restock munitions drained in the conflict in the Gulf.

Legislators have been visiting U.S. military bases in times of conflict since at least 1943, when five U.S. senators embarked on a 65-day inspection tour of global military sites during World War II. Visits increased during and after the Vietnam war, when American lawmakers and journalists returned home with stories that vastly differed from former President Richard Nixon’s narrative that the U.S. was winning the war.

Farkas, who served for eight years as a staff member of the Senate Armed Services Committee and took several trips to the Gulf as part of a congressional delegation (CODEL), said congressional visits to these military bases are a way to not only increase public knowledge of the status of a war overseas, but in many cases justify granting the military additional and targeted resources for specific operations.

During the Iraq war, for example, the U.S. sent a CODEL to the Gulf following improvised explosive devices targeted U.S. personnel in armored vehicles, Farkas recalled. The vehicles were not capable of deflecting the explosives, and following a tour of U.S. military sites, Congress conducted a bipartisan effort to ramp up production of the vehicles.

“It’s legitimate, and also necessary and desirable, for members of Congress to go even during a hot war,” Farkas said.

The Pentagon also has some legitimate reasons for turning lawmakers away from military bases, Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and former director for the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, told Fortune.

Hosting a CODEL requires resources like military aircraft and personnel to protect and move lawmakers. In a military theater, armed forces may be unable to spare resources, and when specific threats are made against the military, both troops and elected representatives can be put in harm’s way. In 2016 under then-President Barack Obama, the military asked Congress to limit visits to Afghanistan during a fighting season, though it was not an express ban. Across both Republican and Democrat administrations, U.S. Central Command has ordered limited visits to military sites.

However, Hegseth’s prohibition of military visits has continued, even after the end of “Operation Epic Fury” in May, and when, prior to this month, the last known U.S. attack on Iran was in September. Typically, restrictions are lifted after “hot phases” of conflict end, and the Pentagon’s decision to turn away legislators even during lulls in attacks is what raised suspicions of ulterior motives beyond protecting troops and lawmakers.

“The big concern I would have is, the administration has said that Operation Epic Fury is over. Is this more of a lack of transparency and an attempt to hide some of the things that are going on, like the destruction of some of the bases?” Dent said.

What has lawmakers and former Pentagon officials scratching their heads is that increased transparency to Congress usually yields additional funding, which appears aligned with Hegseth’s push for a record-setting Pentagon budget in fiscal 2027. The government faces a Dec. 11 funding deadline to pass either full-year appropriations or a stopgap measure through the end of the year.

“Shutting Congress out is not the way to achieve your objectives if you are the Department of Defense,” Farkas said. “If anything, it’s almost a guarantee that you won’t achieve your objectives because Congress understands what their rights and prerogatives are…so that can just erode trust and confidence further.”

Particularly after the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, incoming legislators are going to approach the Pentagon’s steep demands with even more rigor, Fargas noted. President Donald Trump will be reluctant to exercise a veto on the National Defense Authorization Act because it outlines military funding, despite Democrats being likely to make changes to it.

“It’s better to be open and honest,” she said. “You can’t hide these things anyway. You’re going to bring in contractors. You’re going to have to put out bids for repairs. Somewhere this information is going to come to light.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5299. Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.)

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5298. Huawei convicted on 10 counts in U.S. trial, but verdict is unlikely to slow China’s ‘national champion’

A federal jury in New York convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts Tuesday, including bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Yet Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

The verdict caps a U.S. case launched in 2018 that accused the Chinese telecommunications giant of misleading banks about its business in Iran while stealing trade secrets from U.S. companies. Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement.

“Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies,” he added.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that the acquittal on the racketeering charge reflected the company’s “good-faith compliance culture.”

“We fully expect to appeal,” Heberlig told reporters, according to Reuters.

In a statement, Huawei argued that the acquittal on the racketeering charge “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis.” The company also said it believed the other charges “are equally without legal or factual merit,” and that it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and the daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, was arrested in Canada in December 2018 at the request of U.S. authorities. Prosecutors accused her of misleading banks about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, a subsidiary operating in Iran. After nearly three years fighting extradition, she was released in September 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. prosecutors; the charges were later dismissed.

Separately, the U.S. Commerce Department placed Huawei on its Entity List in 2019, restricting its access to American goods, software, and technology. Washington tightened those controls in 2020 to cover certain foreign-made products manufactured using U.S. technology or software.

Tuesday’s verdict is unlikely to slow Huawei, says Dexter Tiff Roberts, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub. “Huawei has already weathered years of sanctions and still been able to grow and develop remarkably, even with limited access to a number of developed country markets and in particular the U.S.”

Beijing may double down on Huawei instead, he adds. “In some ways, the adversity it’s already faced with sanctions [has] made Beijing double down on supporting it as a national champion, and if anything, the latest court ruling will only strengthen Beijing’s resolve to support Huawei to ensure it does not stumble.”

The verdict comes as Huawei takes on a growing role in China’s push to build a domestic AI-computing industry, amid U.S. export controls blocking the country’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. The company’s Ascend semiconductors are China’s best hope for the AI processors needed to train and run models. Chinese models are increasingly being designed to run on Huawei chips, even if Nvidia’s are better for training.

Huawei rotating chair Eric Xu said the company cannot produce enough AI chips and servers to meet demand in mainland China. “Since we don’t have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China, we don’t have a plan to expand into the international market in a fully fledged way,” Xu told reporters at Huawei Connect in Shanghai in September, according to Reuters.

Huawei reported 880.9 billion yuan ($126 billion) in revenue last year, according to its annual report.

#5297. From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

The Sustainability Spotlight profiles individuals who are impacting the future of our planet by turning visionary climate tech concepts into real-world solutions.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm

Since Grant Canary launched his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a new line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the issues.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally important: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

Data and science guide us. Passion and invention drive us. We work backward from ambitious targets because that’s where progress happens, bringing innovation to the planet’s biggest challenges. Every package delivered, every data center powered, every product designed is an opportunity to make tomorrow better—and we share what we learn to help accelerate collective climate action.

#5295. America’s defense budget is being squeezed to its lowest share of the federal budget since World War II as China narrows the military gap

America is approaching a “dangerous moment” for defense spending, according to a new report from Brookings. The think tank warns that rising outlays on Medicaid, Medicare, Social Security, and interest on the $40 trillion national debt are squeezing the military’s share of federal spending.The analysis, published at the start of this week, finds that since 1962 defense spending has been squeezed from 49% to 13% of the federal budget.Defense spending accounted for 2.8% of U.S. GDP in 2026 and is expected to remain at approximately 3% through 2030. This would put defense spending at its lowest share of GDP since World War II, said Brookings—a nonprofit public policy think tank based in D.C.

Projections that spending will remain relatively constrained are particularly concerning, Brookings’ Jessica Riedl writes. The U.S. is engaged in a conflict in the Middle East with Iran and its proxy groups, and Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a land war that has continued since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

Three years ago, the RAND National Security Research Division—a Pentagon research advisor—warned that “in many ways, China is outpacing the United States and has largely negated the U.S. military advantage in the Western Pacific through two decades of focused military investment.”

Without “significant change” in policy, the “balance of power will continue to shift in China’s favor,” the congressional report found.

And yet, in the years since, the factors stacking up against increased defense spending are only getting weightier.

The Congressional Budget Office’s latest roundup of government spending shows that $917 billion was spent on defense for fiscal year 2026, a 5.8% increase of $48 billion from the prior year.

The total for the government’s largest mandatory spending programs (Social Security benefits, Medicare, and Medicaid) came in at nearly $3.5 trillion, a $217 billion uptick on the year before and a 6.7% increase. The government ran a total deficit of $1.9 trillion, the CBO reported, adding to the current national debt burden of $40.7 trillion, per the latest Treasury data.

That debt comes at a cost. Interest payments rise as the government borrows more, particularly when borrowing costs remain elevated. The CBO said that for fiscal year 2026, the Treasury paid $1.14 trillion in net interest on the public debt—an 11.1% or $114 billion increase on the previous fiscal year.

Interest payments on the debt are a growing concern for D.C. policymakers. The U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee (JEC) published a report in October that found interest payments in the future could consume more than half of available federal tax receipts by 2036.

JEC chairman David Schweikert noted: “Under this higher interest rate scenario, we could spend $23 trillion on interest alone over the next decade. That is spending not on Social Security, not on Medicare, not on national defense, but simply paying for yesterday’s borrowing.”

The next Congress faces difficult choices: The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has a countdown to when the combined trust funds of the Social Security system will be forced to start cutting benefits. The countdown currently stands at seven years and six months.

“The newly elected Congress—which controls the purse strings—faces difficult fiscal choices that will persist into the next presidential administration,” the Brookings report says. “Now, there is little headroom in the budget to increase defense spending to meet the proliferating defense challenges … Something will have to give. The advocates of a robust military and American global leadership should prepare to make the most of limited budgetary resources.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5294. Why Is Crypto Down Today? Total Market Cap Crashes -2.5%

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Why Is Crypto Down Today? Cryptocurrency markets woke up red on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Bitcoin slipped below the psychologically important $60,000 level, trading near $59,800–$60,500 after briefly touching levels above $64,000 the day before.

Ethereum, Solana, and most major altcoins followed lower, with the total crypto market capitalization contracting roughly 1–2% over 24 hours amid elevated liquidations and persistent selling pressure. The question on every trader’s mind is straightforward: why is crypto down today?

🚨 IS THE BOTTOM IN?Bitcoin has been through some brutal crashes before.> 84% in 2018.> 77% in 2022.> And a 56% drop from its $126K peak in 2026.So, what happened this time?The market was already loaded with leverage. When Bitcoin started falling, liquidations kicked… pic.twitter.com/ZGjuafXiyd

Crypto entered the week already wounded. Bitcoin had plunged to a multi-year low near $55,000 over the prior weekend, wiping out leveraged positions and leaving the market in extreme fear territory.

Monday brought a sharp relief rally. Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sent the chipmaker’s shares soaring more than 30% and lifted the Nasdaq by around 7%. Risk assets broadly benefited, and Bitcoin briefly joined the party, climbing toward $64,000.

That bounce proved short-lived. By Tuesday morning, the gains had been fully erased. Bitcoin lagged the equity rebound significantly; Nvidia recovered most of its recent losses, while crypto reclaimed only a fraction of its slide. The divergence highlighted that crypto’s problems run deeper than a single day’s equity news.

Several concrete developments converged to pressure prices. First, the Nvidia-driven rally simply faded. Stock futures turned lower on Tuesday as the initial euphoria cooled.

Nasdaq-100 futures dropped around 1%, and related AI and crypto-adjacent equities gave back part of Monday’s gains. Crypto, which had been riding the coattails of the tech surge, sold off in sympathy but more sharply.

Second, institutional flows remained deeply negative. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $570M in net outflows on Monday, the fifth consecutive session of withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT alone accounted for more than $500M of that figure. November’s cumulative outflows reached roughly $4.71Bn, setting a monthly record and removing a major source of structural demand that had previously supported prices.

Third, derivatives markets amplified the move. More than $800M in crypto futures positions were liquidated over the 24-hour period, more than triple the prior day’s total. Forced selling from both long and short positions created a self-reinforcing cascade as prices fell.

Broader macro factors also weighed on sentiment. Markets continue to price in a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with key inflation data (PCE) due shortly.

Higher rates typically pressure non-yielding assets such as Bitcoin. Additional reports of possible new U.S. tariff measures added another layer of risk-off caution. Lingering effects from the large Binance-related hack earlier in the period further eroded confidence in the sector.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Crypto’s decline today is not the result of a single dramatic headline. Instead, it reflects a short-term relief rally that failed to overcome persistent structural headwinds.

The Nvidia news provided temporary momentum, but without positive ETF flows or a meaningful shift in monetary expectations, that momentum evaporated quickly. Leveraged traders were caught offside, and the resulting liquidations accelerated the drop.

Sentiment remains extremely cautious. The Fear & Greed Index sits deep in extreme fear, at around 10/100, and Bitcoin has still only recovered a modest portion of its November losses.

While some long-term holders and selective buyers may view current levels as attractive, the immediate market is dominated by risk reduction and profit-taking after the failed bounce.

Crypto is down today primarily because Monday’s Nvidia-fueled rally proved unsustainable. Heavy, record-setting Bitcoin ETF outflows continued to drain demand, while a surge in futures liquidations forced additional selling.

Macro uncertainty around interest rates and risk assets provided no supporting backdrop. In short, the market tested a bounce, found insufficient real buying interest, and retreated—leaving Bitcoin back below $60,000 and the broader crypto complex lower.

#5293. The White House announced a raft of new tariffs on the same day inflation data came back at nearly twice the Fed’s target

The White House has announced a litany of new tariffs targeting imports from 14 economies, including key trading partners such as China and the EU. With consumers already stretched by an affordability crisis, the new duties come on the same day that the Bureau of Economic Analysis confirmed inflation hit 3.8%, according to the annual rate of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, and nearly double the Federal Open Market Committee’s 2% goal.

The announcement has two important implications. First, though the new duties would be imposed on foreign economies, previous tariff studies indicate that 90% of the increased prices are ultimately borne by U.S. businesses and, more often than not, their consumers.

And second, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s next move. The Fed, now led by Kevin Warsh, raised rates in September for the first time since July 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and meets again Dec. 9–10.

Former Fed chairman Jerome Powell said that while tariffs represented a one-off price increase rather than broader inflationary factors, they nonetheless increased near-term inflation expectations. As UBS chief economist Paul Donovan told clients today: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates.”

And the Fed already has a data headache on its hands: The PCE increase to 3.8% compared with a year ago is nearly double the FOMC’s 2% target.

China faces a new 20% duty, and Vietnam, up to 35%, or 20% if it reaches a trade deal, according to Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, citing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Section 301 allows the U.S. to investigate foreign practices deemed unreasonable or discriminatory, or that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Both nations are among the top 10 importers to the U.S., accounting for 7.8% and 7.4% of imports, respectively, per Census Bureau data.

Through September, the U.S. imported $215 billion in Chinese goods and $204.8 billion from Vietnam, which accounts for the largest U.S. trade deficit with any country, at $190.9 billion.

The European Union is also facing tariffs of 15%, while India is facing rates of up to 25%, or 17% in the event of a trade deal.

The new revenue-generating tariff action comes after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs in February, forcing the administration to refund roughly $100 billion of the $166 billion it had collected.

For most of the 14 economies, existing Section 301 duties count toward the new rate rather than being added on top. (China is the exception: Its 20% stacks on existing levies.) “In effect, it’ll look more like a top-up,” Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points.”

That will do little to calm the nerves of consumers who have been battling above-target inflation for more than five years. The New York Fed’s October survey of consumer expectations revealed that households expect inflation to be at 3.9% this time next year, and at 3.3% in three years’ time.

For the Fed, these heightened expectations can be a problem. Consumers may adjust their spending and saving, and make wage demands in response to their inflation expectations. That can create a self-reinforcing cycle, making inflation harder to bring down.

“The tariffs replace the previously announced Section 301 tariffs with a marginal incremental impact higher on goods prices but, moreover, set the table for further increases if negotiations break down,” Bradford Smith, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told Fortune in a note.

“The announcement serves as a reminder that the Fed’s inflation fight is exacerbated by tariffs. With inflation already an issue and the Fed awaiting the lapping of previous tariff implementations, additional tariffs will make the Fed’s job more difficult.”
